positions.commentary: The speaker mentions GM has the Chevy Bolt coming out next year with a 200-mile range, pure electric, for $30,000.
The speaker notes that if Amazon is a fair value, then Uber's valuation being one-sixth of Amazon raises questions.
The speaker compares a cab driver's focus on Cisco in 2000 to the shoe shine boy in 1929, noting Cisco never reached its market cap again.
The speaker quotes David Einhorn saying Oracle, Microsoft, Apple, and Google have sedate valuations compared to tech slivers.
The speaker questions whether Netflix will still exist in 2068 due to the reconfigurations that take place in rapidly changing industries.
Tesla would not have a car equivalent to GM's Chevy Bolt until at least 2018, putting GM two years ahead despite GM's name recognition issues.
The speaker notes Micron is currently at 15 billion in market cap.
The speaker mentions Facebook has a valuation north of 200 times earnings.
IBM is the sole exception among the tech names in the 1973-74 Nifty 50 that did not disappear, though it did not deliver a good return.
Investors coming into Amazon and Uber today have no memory of the 1973-74 Nifty 50 crash and do not see the parallels.

thesis: This episode argues that many high-flying tech stocks are overvalued relative to their earnings or lack a sustainable business model, citing examples like Netflix's flawed economics and Tesla's heavy capital requirements. The speaker contrasts these 'slivers' with more traditional, cash-generative companies like GM and Cisco, warning that current investors lack the historical perspective to see parallels to past crashes.
